questions.q: Why can a recommender with an excellent RMSE still give users a poor top-10 list?
options: RMSE is always misleading and should never be computed
RMSE measures predicted-rating error across all items, but users only see a ranked list, so ranking metrics are needed too
RMSE only works on implicit feedback data
A low RMSE guarantees a good ranking, so this cannot happen
questions.explain: RMSE scores rating predictions; users see the top of a ranked list. Precision@k, recall@k, and NDCG@k evaluate that list directly.

questions.q: In the offline split shown in the lesson, what is held out for each user?
options: All of the user's history
A random 20% of users
One item the user interacted with, which the model must rank highly
Every item the user has not clicked
questions.explain: Each user keeps most of their history as training data and one interaction is hidden as the test item, mimicking how a real recommender predicts the next interaction.

questions.q: What does NDCG@k reward that plain precision@k does not?
options: Recommending more items than k
Placing relevant items higher in the list, since a hit at position 1 counts more than a hit at position 5
Recommending only unseen items
Covering more of the catalog
questions.explain: NDCG discounts each hit by its rank position, so ordering within the top k matters, whereas precision@k treats all k positions equally.

questions.q: Why do we set already-seen items to minus infinity before taking the top k?
options: So the model is not credited for recommending items the user already has
To make the scores positive
To speed up sorting
To increase catalog coverage artificially
questions.explain: Recommending something a user already interacted with is useless and would inflate the metrics, so seen items are excluded from the ranking.

questions.q: A new model scores only slightly better than recommending the most popular items. What is the best conclusion?
options: The model is fine because it is better than random
Popularity baselines are irrelevant on real data
The complexity may not be justified; validate with an online A/B test before shipping
Precision@k should be replaced with RMSE
questions.explain: The popularity baseline is the bar to clear. A marginal gain offline may not justify complexity, and offline metrics are only a proxy, so confirm with an online experiment.
